about: Test items built from data/asa_cases.json. 'claim' and 'context' are written neutrally: they never state the regulator's verdict or reasoning. 'label' is the UK ASA's ruling on that claim (flawed = upheld/misleading, sound = not upheld). Paraphrased by an AI reader; source is the authority. Layout-only and fear-narrative claims (Pegasus, Taylor Wimpey, Churchill distress narrative) are excluded because they are not reasoning tests.

items.label: flawed
items.claim: A rental factsheet for a residential tower still under construction in central London states estimated average gross yields (1-bed 3.9-4.9%, 2-bed 4.5-4.6%, 3-bed 2.9-3.8%) and estimated weekly rents (1-bed 745-925 GBP, 2-bed 1,115-1,335 GBP, 3-bed 1,750-2,500 GBP), presented as what a buy-to-let investor can expect.
items.context: Evidence the advertiser relied on: asking-price rents from one property portal for one nearby tower, including penthouses, duplexes and homes outside the same postcode. Independent achieved-rent data for that nearby tower (LonRes): 1-bed 700-750 GBP/week, 2-bed 1,100-2,150 GBP/week, 3-bed 2,095-2,308 GBP/week.

items.label: flawed
items.claim: An email to investors about off-plan flats in east London says prices in the area are expected to rise at least 5-10% over the next 18 months and have already done so in the past, which it says equates to a 50-100% return on the actual investment.
items.context: Advertiser's worked example: unit price 430,000 GBP; 10% deposit (43,000 GBP) with nothing more to pay until completion; 5% a year growth over 18 months gives a value of about 462,787 GBP, a gain of 32,787 GBP, a 76% return on the deposit; 10% growth would give about 155%. Support offered: a 2014 newspaper article reporting that average house prices in the whole borough rose 43% between May 2013 and May 2014.

items.label: flawed
items.claim: A paid social media ad for land auction investments states a 10-30% ROI.
items.context: Evidence the advertiser supplied: two case studies. Case 1 (subdivided in September 2021): a plot valued at 25,000 GBP sold for 48,500 GBP and was split into lots totalling 138,500 GBP. Case 2 (subdivided May 2024): a plot valued at 950,000 GBP was split into 20 lots totalling 1,242,000 GBP (30% increase).

items.label: flawed
items.claim: A land-auction website states that selling land at auction achieves a much higher price than selling through a local estate agent.
items.context: The comparison uses auction sale prices on one side and, on the other, figures the advertiser describes as local estate agent valuations of the same kind of land. No data is shown on whether the auction method caused any price difference.

items.label: flawed
items.claim: Paid social ads and a landing page for a land-investment mentoring course state that clients made 6,000,000 GBP in profit this year, that one client made a profit on a 350K land deal, and that profits of 100,000 GBP up to half a million GBP are possible, with six-figure profits described as achievable.
items.context: No client records, sales data or averages are provided with the claims.

items.label: flawed
items.claim: A retirement-property web page states that downsizing from a three-bedroom house to one of its apartments saves over 1,000 GBP a year on energy (a video on the page cites 1,160 GBP).
items.context: The comparison apartment was in a development rated B for energy efficiency with a ground-source heat pump. The comparison houses were assumed to use 24,255 kWh and 27,560 kWh a year; Ofgem's typical figures are 14,200 kWh (medium household) and 21,100 kWh (high). The ad does not say which apartments or heating type the saving applies to.

items.label: flawed
items.claim: The same web page and a paid social post state that downsizing to one of its retirement homes saves about 2,300 GBP a year on average in total.
items.context: The company's estimate ranged from 2,260 to 2,740 GBP. Its comparison homes were assumed to use 24,255 and 27,560 kWh a year of energy against Ofgem's typical 14,200 kWh (medium) and 21,100 kWh (high). The apartments used in the comparison used about 25% less energy than the average in their development. The ad does not explain the basis.

items.label: flawed
items.claim: An estate agent's leaflet states 'up to 10% higher sale prices than other local estate agents', with a footnote saying it has completed sales at up to 10% above the figure at which other local agents initially valued the property.
items.context: Evidence supplied: the agent had completed 13 sales since opening; two were more than 10% above another agent's initial valuation; examples given were 10.8%, 10.6% and 5.9% above initial valuation. Support consisted of emails from some of the vendors saying other agents had valued their homes lower.

items.label: flawed
items.claim: The same leaflet states 'we are the only local estate agent open seven days a week'.
items.context: The leaflet was delivered to one village. 'Local' is not defined. A neighbouring town very close by has several estate agents, some of which are open on Sundays. The advertiser says it is the only agent open seven days a week in its own village.

items.label: sound
items.claim: The leaflet, which was posted to every home in the village including some who had already instructed a rival agent, does not warn that a vendor who has signed a sole-agency contract with another agent could owe two sets of fees if they switch.
items.context: Estate agents are already required to explain sole-agency terms and fee liabilities to vendors when they sign up. The leaflet was a general mailing, not aimed at any specific rival's properties.

items.label: flawed
items.claim: An online estate agent's website claims a 4,158 GBP average customer saving when selling, based on its average sale price with the UK average commission rate of 1.5% applied.
items.context: Evidence supplied: the average UK asking price (from a property advertising website, March 2016) of 303,190 GBP; the 1.5% average commission was taken from an email by one national conveyancing firm; the agent's own fixed fees are 798 GBP outside London and 1,158 GBP in Greater London (including VAT). No sales data of the agent's own was supplied to show its average sale price or how the figure was calculated.

items.label: sound
items.claim: A TV ad for the same online estate agent shows a client being told 'you could save thousands', with small print citing average estate agent commission from a 2011 Which? survey.
items.context: The Which? survey (2011) reported commissions between 0.75% and 3.5% with a national average of 1.8%. The agent charges one of two fixed fees (798 GBP outside London, 1,158 GBP inside, including VAT). A property valued at 300,000 GBP would pay 3,000 GBP commission at 1%.

items.label: sound
items.claim: A franchise estate agent's leaflet comparison table lists 'your personal agent all the way' as something it offers and that three named competitors do not.
items.context: The table has nine rows, ticked for the advertiser on all nine and for the competitors on two. A footnote says it is based on research of each agency's standard package, with no sources or date. The advertiser's model has a single named agent for each client from valuation to completion.

items.label: sound
items.claim: The same table lists 'accompanied viewings by your personal agent' as an advertiser feature that the three named competitors do not offer.
items.context: Same nine-row table and footnote (research of each agency's standard package, no sources or date). The advertiser says its agents accompany viewings.

items.label: sound
items.claim: The same leaflet states '#1 in the world for home sales volume!' in the context of the RE/MAX brand.
items.context: The claim sits in the advertiser's own marketing next to the brand name; no competitor figures are shown on the page.

items.label: flawed
items.claim: The table lists 'personal social media campaign' as a feature the advertiser has and the three named competitors do not.
items.context: Same nine-row table with a footnote citing research of each agency's standard package, no sources or date. Estate agents commonly list homes on social media.

items.label: flawed
items.claim: The table lists 'personalised sale board for maximum marketing effect' as a feature the advertiser has and the three named competitors do not.
items.context: Same nine-row table with an unsourced research footnote. Sale boards with agency branding are widely used by estate agents.

items.label: flawed
items.claim: The table lists 'same day feedback on all viewings' as a feature the advertiser guarantees and the three named competitors do not.
items.context: Same nine-row table with an unsourced research footnote. No data on the advertiser's or competitors' actual feedback times is shown.

items.label: flawed
items.claim: The table lists 'skilled negotiations by an agent who knows your home' as a feature the advertiser has and the three named competitors do not.
items.context: Same nine-row table with an unsourced research footnote. No measure of negotiating skill is given.

items.label: flawed
items.claim: A magazine ad for holiday lodges on UK resorts, priced from 295,000 GBP, headlines a guaranteed return of up to about 83,000 GBP over two years, 'based on historical success'.
items.context: Terms found elsewhere on the advertiser's site: the guarantee belongs to an optional sublet plan, requires 80% minimum occupancy, runs for 12 to 24 months, and any shortfall is made up after 12 months. The ad does not mention these terms. Ongoing service charge, utilities and insurance apply to owners but are not mentioned in the ad.

items.label: flawed
items.claim: The same ad presents the lodge as an investment with a guaranteed return and refers to 'historical success'. The ad text contains no statement about the value of the lodge possibly falling, and no statement about past performance.
items.context: The ad was published in a national newspaper magazine for a general audience.

items.label: flawed
items.claim: The social media ad promoting land auction investments with a stated 10-30% ROI contains no statement that the value of land investments can go down as well as up.
items.context: The ad was aimed at property and land investors via a mailing-list sign-up.

items.label: flawed
items.claim: The mentoring ads promise six-figure profits and 'financial freedom' from land investing and contain no statement that land values can fall and no statement that past results are not a guide to future results. A web page does carry a small-print disclaimer, but the paid social ads do not.
items.context: The ads were seen as paid social media posts by a general audience.

items.label: flawed
items.claim: The investor email promising a 50-100% return on off-plan flats says prices 'have already done so in the past' and contains no statement that property values can fall or that past performance is not a guide to the future.
items.context: The email went to a list of prospective property investors.
